neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; oriented to month and year but not exact date. MMSE 22/30, losing points on recall (0/3 at 5 minutes), orientation (2 points lost), and serial sevens (2 errors). Clock drawing shows mildly disorganized number placement with hands set to incorrect time. Unable to recall 3 words after 5 minutes even with categorical cues. Naming intact for high-frequency items but hesitates on low-frequency items (e.g., 'stethoscope'). Repetition intact. Comprehension intact for simple commands, mild difficulty with multi-step commands.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Face symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. No dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, normal base, normal stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp reflex. No myoclonus. Anosmia not tested.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss over the past two years, worsening over the last six months
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Margaret Thornton is a 72-year-old right-handed retired elementary school teacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband, Robert, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past two years. Her husband reports that he first began noticing subtle changes approximately two years ago when she started repeating questions she had asked minutes earlier and occasionally forgetting recent conversations with family members. Over the past year, the symptoms have become more pronounced. She has missed two scheduled hair salon appointments, which her husband describes as very unlike her, as she has kept the same standing appointment for over twenty years. She has difficulty recalling the names of acquaintances she has known for years, though she recognizes their faces. At their weekly bridge club, which she has attended for fifteen years, her partner recently commented that Margaret seems to lose track of which cards have been played, something that never happened before. Her husband also notes that she has become more reliant on written lists for grocery shopping, whereas she previously managed the household shopping from memory. She left a pot of water boiling on the stove unattended on two occasions in the past three months, prompting her husband to begin monitoring the kitchen more closely. She has not gotten lost while driving on familiar routes, but her husband has taken over driving on longer trips because she seemed anxious navigating highways. She continues to dress and groom herself independently and manages her personal hygiene without difficulty. She is aware that her memory is not what it used to be and appears frustrated and mildly anxious about the changes. There have been no episodes of confusion, hallucinations, personality changes, or behavioral disturbances. She denies headache, seizures, falls, tremor, or difficulty walking. Sleep has been unremarkable, with no REM sleep behavior reported by her husband. Her mood has been somewhat subdued but she denies persistent sadness or anhedonia.

differential_by_imaging.rationale: Bilateral hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens grade 2-3) with temporoparietal-predominant cortical volume loss is the hallmark neuroimaging pattern of Alzheimer's disease
Fazekas grade 1 periventricular white matter changes; no strategic infarcts identified
Atrophy is temporoparietal-predominant rather than frontal or anterior temporal

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile. Significant impairment in verbal learning and delayed recall (RAVLT delayed recall 1st percentile; immediate recall 5th percentile) consistent with a storage-type memory deficit. Semantic fluency (10th percentile) and executive function (Trail Making B, 20th percentile) are below expected norms. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 25th percentile) and basic processing speed (Trail Making A) are preserved. Screening scores: MMSE 22/30, MoCA 18/30. Clinical correlation recommended.

alzheimer_management.query: early-onset Alzheimer disease management cholinesterase inhibitors

results.title: Practice guideline update summary: Mild cognitive impairment
results.authors: Petersen RC, Lopez O, Armstrong MJ, et al.
results.summary: Evidence-based guidelines for MCI and early Alzheimer disease management including pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions.

alzheimer_management.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated modest cognitive and functional benefits in mild to moderate Alzheimer disease in randomized controlled trials. Non-pharmacological approaches including cognitive stimulation and caregiver support have also shown benefit in controlled studies.

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral medial-temporal / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism characteristic of Alzheimer pattern

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

key_educational_points: Early AD presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Reversible causes of dementia must always be excluded with laboratory testing
Hippocampal atrophy on MRI is a supportive but not pathognomonic finding
CSF biomarkers (Abeta42, phospho-tau, total tau) can confirm AD pathology in vivo
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate AD
